title: A Cheap Chinese AI Model Is Catching America's Best. India's Tech Sector Is in the Crossfire.
excerpt: Beijing-based Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 nearly matches OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost — and US restrictions on its own models are making the problem worse.
body:
A cheap, powerful AI model from Beijing is climbing the global usage charts faster than DeepSeek did — and this time, the threat to American dominance may be harder to dismiss.

GLM-5.2, built by Chinese startup Zhipu AI (also known as Z.ai), launched last month and has Silicon Valley in a state of nervous admiration. The model's coding and agentic capabilities — its ability to plan, execute, and iterate through complex tasks with minimal human prompting — nearly rival those of the leading American offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, at roughly one-sixth the cost.

"We now have a Chinese open-weight model that is as good as the currently available models from OpenAI and Anthropic," said David Sacks, former US AI czar under President Trump, on the All-In podcast. "It is just a tick below Opus 4.8 and right up there with GPT 5.5."

## The Numbers Tell the Story

GLM-5.2 currently sits fifth on Artificial Analysis' large language model intelligence leaderboard, which ranks performance across reasoning, coding, and general capability benchmarks. On Code Arena's front-end coding rankings — measuring how well models generate websites and applications — it holds second place globally.


![Silicon Valley — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg)


On OpenRouter, a popular third-party platform where developers pick AI models, token traffic for GLM-5.2 is climbing faster than it did after DeepSeek's V4 launch in April. Executives from Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy to venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have publicly praised its abilities.

"Genuinely impressed, almost shocked, at how good GLM 5.2 is at coding," tweeted Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel. "This changes things."



> **""Genuinely impressed, almost shocked, at how good GLM 5.2 is at coding," tweeted Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel."**


## Why This One Is Different

DeepSeek's debut early last year triggered a global tech selloff but ultimately faded as markets decided it was a one-off chatbot scare. GLM-5.2 is different. It's built for agentic work — planning, coding, testing, and looping through multi-step tasks autonomously — which is exactly the kind of labour enterprises are desperately trying to automate.

As AI token spending has ballooned beyond what many companies budgeted, intelligence per dollar has become the metric that matters. A model that delivers near-frontier performance at a fifth of the price is not a curiosity. It's a competitive threat.


![David Sacks — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ea/David_Sacks_in_March_2025.jpg)


Security researchers have found that GLM-5.2 can match Anthropic's Mythos model in cybersecurity tasks — specifically, finding bugs in software code. The Wall Street Journal reported that Zhou Hongyi, founder of China's 360 Security, unveiled AI tools built on the model at a Beijing conference, calling them "Mythos made in China."

## The Self-Inflicted US Wound

The timing is particularly painful for Washington. The Trump administration recently ordered Anthropic to restrict access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for non-US users, citing security concerns. OpenAI was asked to stagger the release of GPT-5.6. These restrictions have inadvertently fuelled global demand for the Chinese alternative.

"The international developer community is increasingly aware that relying solely on proprietary, US-based API models carries significant risk," said Brian Tse, founder of Beijing-based consultancy Concordia AI.

Critics argue the administration's approach is counterproductive — restricting American models while simultaneously allowing exports of AI chips to China, the very hardware powering models like GLM-5.2.


![President Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)


## What This Means for India

The implications for India's technology sector are layered. Indian IT services companies — Infosys, TCS, Wipro — are under pressure to integrate AI into their offerings. Cheaper, more accessible models like GLM-5.2 could accelerate adoption among Indian enterprises that have been priced out of frontier US models.

India's own AI startups stand to benefit from the open-source paradigm that GLM-5.2 represents. With models that can be downloaded, modified, and deployed on local infrastructure, Indian developers can build without the recurring costs and regulatory uncertainty of closed US APIs.

For the diaspora — particularly the thousands of Indian-origin engineers and executives running AI teams at American tech companies — the moment is bittersweet. The models they're building are being constrained by their own government's policies, while a Chinese competitor grows stronger in the gap.

"Developers tend to care less about where a model comes from than whether it works, how much it costs, and whether they can deploy it reliably," said Poe Zhao, China tech analyst. "The likely pattern is partial routing, not overnight replacement. But yes, it is a mini DeepSeek moment."

**Sources:** Reuters, Wall Street Journal, The Street, CNBC, Artificial Analysis, OpenRouter
